article_title: Dependency Cooldowns Spread From pnpm and pip to Bundler, Dependabot and GitHub's Package Firewall While Critics Question the Approach

content_preview.title: Dependency Cooldowns Spread From pnpm and pip to Bundler, Dependabot and GitHub's Package Firewall While Critics Question the Approach
content_preview.summary: Sources describe package-install delays appearing in pnpm, pip, Bundler, Dependabot and GitHub's firewall with differing defaults, alongside an LWN-reported dispute over cooldowns versus upload queues.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Background

A dependency cooldown is a delay between the day a package version is published and the day a build tool or update bot will use it. The idea is to give security researchers and maintainers time to spot a malicious release before it reaches developer machines and CI pipelines. As [LWN.net](https://lwn.net/Articles/1068692/) described it in an April 22, 2026 article, one method of avoiding supply-chain attacks is to add a delay of a few days before pulling updates, in what is known ...

editor_notes.content_quality: Genuine Analysis: examines a trend across five tools (pnpm 11 RC, pip 26.1, Bundler 4.0.13, Dependabot, GitHub package firewall) and a named disagreement (Paterson vs Woodruff, cooldowns vs upload queues). Structure Background / Current situation with 'Disagreement over the approach' subsection / Implications. 1,241 words (range 800-2000). Implications are explicitly framed as drawn from the sources, with no prediction or Herald opinion; they state what the sources do not establish.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read all 7 snapshots (source-0..6.html.gz, all status 200, no archive fallback, no suspicious_patterns) and live re-fetched both GitHub changelog entries on 2026-10-24. source-0 (GitHub changelog, Dependabot): 'at least three days', default on github.com across supported ecosystems, security updates open immediately, cooldown option in dependabot.yml, GHES 3.23 - all confirmed verbatim; live matches. source-1 (GitHub changelog, package firewall): Enterprise Cloud public preview, admin policy controls incl. configurable cooldown, coding agents/CI-CD hosts as endpoints, free in preview, metered billing at GA, npm only - confirmed in snapshot and live as of Oct 24, 2026. The article does not assert the 1-day firewall default in its body (that default is in the docs page cited by the earlier Herald Briefing; the changelog says only 'configurable cooldown period'), so the Briefing and this article are consistent. source-2 (LWN, Apr 22, 2026, Brockmeier): Woodruff Nov 2025 post on ten attacks, <1 week window, 7-day cooldown; Nesbitt March round-up with 'at least ten different configuration names across the tools that do support it'; Paterson Apr 13 argument, free-riding, 'Make new packages wait some period of time after they are published, before they are distributed.', 'I don't want my security to depend on someone else getting hacked first' (Paterson, quoted by LWN); Woodruff reply on Lobste.rs 'directionally accurate', security companies 'financially incentivized', agreed upload queues more desirable but hard to take away; PyPI had not announced upload-queue plans - all confirmed, speakers correctly attributed. source-3 (LWN brief, Jun 5, 2026): Bundler 4.0.13, cooldown filter, opt-in - confirmed. source-4 (InfoQ, Apr 21, 2026, pnpm 11 RC): minimumReleaseAge defaults to 1 day (24 hours); HN debate about whether a grace period helps; commenter warning that delays slow critical security patches - confirmed (the commenters are anonymous HN users, and the article attributes them only as 'commenters'). source-5 (InfoQ, May 20, 2026, pip 26.1): --uploaded-prior-to=P7D example, 8/10 and 14-day figures from Woodruff, Essential Plugin (eight months dormant) and XZ not caught by 7-day cooldown, tradeoff for security fixes and pairing with Dependabot/pip-audit - confirmed. source-6 (The Register, Apr 11, 2026): Trivy and Axios compromises; Ben Read (Wiz, leads cyber threat intel team) 'In all of the cases, they were found in less than 12 hours' about four open-source compromises by TeamPCP - verbatim confirmed. All hosts exact-match allowlist (lwn.net, infoq.com, theregister.com, github.blog); no allowlist change needed. INDEPENDENT-SOURCE COUNT: 7 sources total = 2 vendor (GitHub changelogs, not counted) + 5 independent articles from 3 independent outlets (LWN x2, InfoQ x2, The Register x1). Honest discount: LWN is original reporting and summarises named critics and the cooldown's proponent; its cooldown-debate sources (Woodruff, Paterson) are commentators, not the maintainers of the adopting tools, so not interested parties in the adoption. InfoQ's pnpm and pip pieces are largely relays of release notes and a maintainer's (Richard Si, pip committer) blog post plus HN/Reddit commentary, so they are weaker as independent evidence of the adoption facts but are independent outlets and are used mainly for the counterpoints and Woodruff statistics. The Register is independent but only supplies background on the compromises. Even with the InfoQ pieces treated as secondary, LWN (original) and The Register plus InfoQ yield at least 3 independent outlets; requirement of >=4 sources and >=2 independent met. The Herald's own earlier articles do not count and are not counted.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: No fabricated or misattributed claims found. Tool/version/date attributions correct (pnpm 11 RC 1 day; pip 26.1 opt-in via explicit option; Bundler 4.0.13 opt-in; Dependabot 3-day default dated Jul 14, 2026; firewall preview dated Oct 20, 2026). 'Spread from pnpm and pip to Bundler, Dependabot and the firewall' is supported by a separate source for each adoption, not inferred; the title does not assert causality between the Trivy/Axios compromises and the adoption, and the body only places them as separate background. 'Critics question the approach' is supported by named critic Cal Paterson (via LWN) plus HN commenters (via InfoQ). Source ages (April-June 2026) are stated honestly in the closing note; availability/pricing statement 'as read on October 24, 2026' verified against the live GitHub page. Minor looseness, not requiring a correction: 'Implications' sentence that ten configuration names 'suggests' settings are named differently is a mild inference labelled as analysis. Four internal links (/article/2026-04/22-pnpm-11-rc..., /article/2026-06/07-rubys-bundler..., /article/2026-07/20-github-makes-a-three-day..., /article/2026-10/21-github-puts-a-package-firewall...) all resolve to existing published articles and are described accurately. No orphan body URLs: all 7 body source URLs are in article.sources.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral, attributes every position to a named speaker or outlet, no prediction or Herald opinion; Implications section explicitly says it is drawn from the sources.
editor_notes.originality: New angle: cross-tool trend and the cooldown versus upload-queue debate. Individual adoptions were covered earlier by the Herald as single-release Briefings (pnpm 11 RC, Bundler, Dependabot, package firewall); this article synthesises them and adds the dispute, so it is not a duplicate.
concerns: Several sources (pnpm and pip InfoQ pieces) are relays of release notes; adoption facts for pnpm/pip rest on secondary reporting, which the article attributes accordingly.
Source dates are months old; the article states this honestly.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Meets all Analysis requirements (1,241 words, 7 sources, 3 independent outlets, topic examination, facts separated from analysis). All quotes, numbers, dates and attributions verified against raw snapshots and, for GitHub pages, live. Approved as an Analysis. Featured candidacy: 1 - accurate cross-tool synthesis and debate summary for a defined developer audience, built mostly on existing coverage
